Day 52 of 100 · Linux Administration

Linux Hardening

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityLinux AdministrationPublished artifact recovered

Linux hardening reduces exposed services and privilege while keeping the effective security state observable and supportable.

Architecture / mental model

service inventory → remove/disable unnecessary services → firewall default deny → SSH/identity controls → MAC policy → verification

How it works

The first step is inventory: `ss -lntup` and running-service listings reveal what the host is actually exposing. Every listening port should have an owner and a reason.

Unused services can be stopped/disabled, with masking reserved for cases where a service must not be started manually or as a dependency. UFW can then enforce default-deny inbound behavior while allowing only required services.

Mandatory-access-control systems such as AppArmor or SELinux should be inspected and understood. Disabling them because a denial appeared trades a useful security boundary for convenience.

Hands-on reference

sudo ss -lntup
systemctl --type=service --state=running
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose
sudo aa-status
getenforce
sestatus

Verification

From another host, test only the intended ports. On the server, re-run listener and firewall inspection and confirm disabled services do not return after reboot.

Field note / gotcha

A firewall rule cannot protect a service you forgot was listening on another interface or port. Inventory comes before hardening claims.

Security considerations

Use key-based SSH, least privilege, patching, service minimization and effective-state verification rather than one-time checklist completion.

What I learned

A hardened server runs less, exposes less and makes each remaining privilege deliberate.
